title: Chapter 24
paragraphs: "Well, was it nice?" she asked, coming out to meet him with a meek, apologetic look.

"Just the usual," he answered, seeing at a glance that she was in one of her good moods. He was used to these swings by now, and he was particularly pleased to see it today, as he was in an unusually good mood himself.
"What's this? Now, that's something!" he said, pointing at the boxes in the passage.
"Yes, we have to go. I went out for a drive, and it was so lovely I longed to be in the country. There's nothing keeping you, is there?"
"It's the one thing I want. I'll be right back and we'll talk it over; I only want to change my coat. Order some tea."
And he went into his room.

There was something mortifying in his "Now, that's something" — the way you'd say it to a child who has stopped being naughty — and still more mortifying was the contrast between her contrite tone and his self-confident one. For a moment the urge to fight flared up in her again, but with an effort she beat it down and met Vronsky as good-humoredly as before.
When he came back she told him — partly using sentences she had prepared in advance — how she had spent the day, and her plans for going.

"You know, it came to me almost like an inspiration," she said. "Why wait here for the divorce? Won't it be just the same in the country? I can't wait any longer! I don't want to keep hoping, I don't want to hear another word about the divorce. I've made up my mind it won't have any more bearing on my life. Do you agree?"
"Oh, yes!" he said, glancing uneasily at her keyed-up face.
"What did you do? Who was there?" she asked after a pause.

Vronsky named the guests. "The dinner was first-rate, and so was the boat race, and the whole thing was pleasant enough, but in Moscow they can never do anything without something _ridicule_. A lady of a sort turned up — swimming instructor to the Queen of Sweden — and gave us a demonstration of her skill."
"How? She swam?" Anna asked, frowning.
"In some absurd red _costume de natation;_ and she was old and ugly too. So when are we going?"
"What an absurd thing! Why, did she swim in some special way?" Anna asked, ignoring his question.
"There was absolutely nothing to it. That's just my point — it was awfully stupid. Well then, when do you mean to go?"
Anna shook her head as though trying to shake off an unwelcome thought.
"When? Why, the sooner the better! By tomorrow we won't be ready. The day after."

"Yes... oh, no, wait — the day after tomorrow is Sunday, I have to be at maman's," said Vronsky, awkwardly, because the moment he said his mother's name he felt her staring, suspicious eyes on him. His awkwardness only confirmed her suspicion. She flushed hotly and drew back from him. It wasn't the Queen of Sweden's swimming instructor that filled Anna's imagination now — it was the young Princess Sorokina, who was staying in a village near Moscow with Countess Vronskaya.
"Can't you go tomorrow?" she said.
"Well, no. The deeds and the money I'm going for can't be ready by tomorrow," he answered.
"In that case, we won't go at all."
"But why?"
"I won't go any later. Monday or never!"
"What for?" Vronsky said, as though astonished. "There's no sense in it!"

"There's no sense in it to you, because you don't care about me. You don't care to understand my life. The one thing here I cared about was Hannah. You say it's a pose. Why, yesterday you said I don't love my own daughter, that I love this English girl instead, that it's unnatural. I'd like to know what life would be natural for me!"

For an instant she saw clearly what she was doing, and was horrified at how far she had fallen from her resolve. But even knowing that this was her own ruin, she could not stop herself, could not keep from proving to him that he was in the wrong, could not give in to him.
"I never said that. I said I didn't sympathize with this sudden passion of yours."
"How can you, when you make so much of your straightforwardness, not tell the truth?"
"I never boast and I never tell lies," he said slowly, holding down his rising anger. "It's a great pity if you can't respect...."
"Respect was invented to fill the empty space where love used to be. And if you don't love me anymore, it would be better and more honest to say so."

"No, this is becoming unbearable!" Vronsky cried, getting up from his chair. He stopped facing her and said deliberately, "What do you try my patience for?" He looked as though he could have said much more, but was holding himself back. "It has its limits."
"What do you mean by that?" she cried, looking with terror at the open hatred in his whole face, and most of all in his cruel, threatening eyes.
"I was going to say...." he began, then stopped himself. "I have to ask what it is you want from me."

"What can I want? All I can want is that you not leave me, the way you are thinking of doing," she said, understanding everything he had not said. "But I don't really want even that — that's secondary. I want love, and there isn't any. So then everything is over."
She turned toward the door.

"Stop! Sto-op!" said Vronsky, no change in the gloomy lines of his brow, though he caught her by the hand. "What is this all about? I said we have to put off going for three days, and on that you tell me I'm lying, that I'm not an honorable man."

"Yes, and I'll say again that a man who reproaches me for having given up everything for him," she said, dredging up the words of an even earlier quarrel, "is worse than a dishonorable man — he's a heartless one."
"Oh, there are limits to what one can put up with!" he shouted, and dropped her hand.

"He hates me, that's plain," she thought, and without a word or a backward glance she walked unsteadily out of the room. "He loves another woman, that's even plainer," she said to herself as she went into her own room. "I want love, and there isn't any. So then, everything is over." She said again the words she had just spoken: "and it must be ended."
"But how?" she asked herself, and sat down in a low chair before the looking-glass.

Thoughts of where to go now — to the aunt who had brought her up, to Dolly, or simply abroad alone — and of what _he_ was doing now, alone in his study; whether this was the final quarrel or whether reconciliation was still possible; and of what all her old friends in Petersburg would say of her now; and of how Alexey Alexandrovitch would look at it, and a great many other notions about what would come after this rupture — all crowded into her head; but she did not give herself fully to any of them. At the bottom of her heart was some dim idea that alone interested her, and she could not bring it into focus. Thinking again of Alexey Alexandrovitch, she remembered the time of her illness after the birth, and the feeling that had never left her then. "Why didn't I die?" and those words and that feeling came back. And suddenly she knew what was in her soul. Yes — it was the idea that solved everything. "Yes, to die!... And the shame and disgrace for Alexey Alexandrovitch and for Seryozha, and my own dreadful shame — death will save us all from it. To die! And he will be filled with remorse; he'll be sorry; he'll love me; he'll suffer for me." With the trace of a self-pitying smile she sat down in the armchair, taking off and putting on the rings on her left hand, picturing vividly from every angle his feelings after her death.
Approaching footsteps — his footsteps — broke her train of thought. As though absorbed in fitting her rings, she did not even turn toward him.
He came up to her, took her hand, and said softly:
"Anna, we'll go the day after tomorrow if you like. I agree to everything."
She did not answer.
"What is it?" he pressed.
"You know," she said, and at that same instant, unable to hold back any longer, she burst into sobs.

"Throw me out!" she got out between sobs. "I'll go away tomorrow... I'll do more. What am I? An immoral woman! A stone around your neck. I don't want to make you miserable, I don't! I'll set you free. You don't love me — you love somebody else!"
Vronsky begged her to calm down and declared there wasn't the slightest basis for her jealousy; that he had never stopped, and never would stop, loving her; that he loved her more than ever.

"Anna, why torment yourself and me like this?" he said, kissing her hands. There was tenderness in his face now, and she thought she heard tears in his voice and felt them wet on her hand. And in an instant Anna's desperate jealousy turned into a desperate flood of tenderness. She threw her arms around him and covered his head, his neck, his hands with kisses.
